title: Diversity Over Frequency: Rethinking Tool Use in Visual Chain-of-Thought Agents
one_liner: Better visual reasoning comes from exploring more different action paths during training, not from forcing the agent to call tools more often.
lead: Visual reasoning agents can call external tools to inspect local image regions or gather extra evidence. A natural guess is that more tool calls should produce better performance because extra evidence can help the agent resolve local uncertainty. This paper shows that the relationship is weaker than it looks. Agents often reduce tool use over training and still get better because training can improve the quality of their reasoning paths even while the final policy calls tools less often. The important factor is not raw tool-call count, but whether training preserves diverse reasoning rollouts instead of collapsing onto a narrow set of repeated behaviors.

problem.h2: Why more tool calls do not automatically mean better reasoning
paras: In visual chain-of-thought systems, tools can zoom in, inspect regions, or provide local evidence. Because tools bring extra information, one might expect that encouraging more tool use would steadily improve performance. The paper finds that this is not what happens in harder tasks such as spatial reasoning and medical visual question answering.

The surprising observation is a tool-use collapse phenomenon: the agent gradually uses tools less often while still improving task accuracy. That means frequency alone is the wrong target. The real question becomes which training signal preserves useful exploration while the model learns when tools matter.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Optimize for diverse rollout exploration rather than high tool frequency, because broad exploration helps the agent discover better reasoning strategies.

steps.b: Study tool use in hard visual reasoning tasks
steps.text: Move beyond simple visual search and test settings where local tool evidence must be combined with global context.
Track how tool usage changes during training and compare it with final accuracy.

steps.b: Test direct encouragement of tool use
steps.text: Reward tool calls and observe whether more usage actually improves reasoning quality because higher call count alone may or may not widen the explored reasoning paths.
Add a diversity term so that training keeps a wider set of candidate reasoning behaviors alive.
Check whether diversity-focused training beats both vanilla training and direct tool-use encouragement.

paras: The paper changes the training target. Instead of treating tool frequency as the main sign of good reasoning, it treats diversity of explored action paths as the quantity worth preserving.
object.object: The exploration objective during visual-agent training

hidden.name: How many genuinely different reasoning and tool-use paths remain available during training
paras: The hidden quantity is rollout diversity. Two agents can make the same number of tool calls, yet one may explore many distinct reasoning paths while the other repeats a narrow pattern with only superficial variation. Raw frequency cannot tell these cases apart.

The paper argues that diversity matters because training needs enough exploration to discover useful ways to combine local tool evidence with the full image context. If exploration collapses too early, the agent may settle on a narrow habit that gives decent scores but misses stronger strategies because those alternatives were never explored long enough to be learned.

heat.caption: High values mark the places where preserving many candidate paths matters more than counting tool calls.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is how wide the agent's search over possible reasoning paths remains while it is learning.
Entropy regularization preserves rollout diversity, which improves training because the agent keeps exploring alternative ways to use tools and context.

paras: Diversity-focused training helps because the agent needs broad exploration to discover strong reasoning plans. A narrow policy may call tools often, yet still fail to test better ways of combining local evidence with the global image because it repeats a small set of familiar paths.

An entropy term helps by resisting early collapse. That does not mean the final agent must use tools more. It means training spends longer exploring the action space, so the best surviving strategy is chosen from a richer set of candidates. Performance improves because the search process during training is better, not because tool frequency is higher.

stages.s: Visual reasoning task with optional external tools
Generate many possible reasoning and tool-use rollouts
Use entropy regularization to keep those rollouts diverse
Select stronger policies after broader exploration because the training search covered more candidate paths
Higher final task accuracy even if tool usage falls later

math.words: Train the agent for task success, but add an entropy bonus over action choices so that the policy does not collapse too quickly onto one narrow pattern of reasoning and tool use.
symbols: the task-success part of the objective
a measure of how spread out the agent's action choices remain

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the agent has three possible next actions: inspect region A, inspect region B, or answer now.
A collapsed policy puts almost all probability on one action and rarely tries the others.
That policy has low entropy, so the diversity term is small.
A broader policy spreads probability across several useful actions and receives a larger entropy bonus during training.
The larger bonus matters because the agent keeps exploring longer and can discover stronger final strategies.

math.note: The real training details are richer, but the direct idea is simple: preserve exploration breadth while the agent is still learning.

charts.title: Encourage more tool calls
charts.note: Using tools more often does not help much when the policy repeats the same narrow patterns because frequency alone does not widen the search over reasoning paths.

charts.title: Encourage rollout diversity
charts.note: The model performs better because broader exploration uncovers stronger reasoning paths during training.

items.b: Too much diversity can delay convergence.
items.html: If exploration stays wide for too long, the agent may waste training effort on weak paths because the policy does not narrow down fast enough.

items.b: Tool collapse may still hide real problems.
items.html: A drop in tool use is not always harmless because the agent may stop checking local evidence even when the task truly needs it.

items.b: Frequency is still useful as a diagnostic.
items.html: The paper shows frequency is not the main target, but tracking it still matters because an unexplained drop can signal that the agent no longer consults evidence when it should.
Measure both exploration diversity and final task quality, and test tasks where tools really matter so that the method is judged on whether broader exploration leads to better reasoning.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a visual reasoning agent that can inspect local image crops before answering. Train one version with a reward for using tools more often and another version with a diversity bonus over action rollouts. Keep the base model, tasks, and tools fixed across both settings.

The demo should prove that rollout diversity is the more useful target because the diversity-trained agent reaches better final task performance even when its final tool-call count is lower than the tool-frequency-trained agent.
demo.metric_eq: diversity_gain = final_score_diverse_training - final_score_tool_frequency_training ; collapse_gap = rollout_entropy_diverse_training - rollout_entropy_tool_frequency_training
demo.closing: A useful demo shows that the best training signal rewards broader search, not just more button presses.
